These various passages are based on definitive statements; however, since those in training who turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle] and those who undergo the transformation of death (parināmikī cyuti) are both indeterminate, these do not obstruct the designation "exit."
If it were not so, they would not have requested the chariots; yet if they had not requested them, how could they have been granted the prediction?

If one says that even while remaining at home they may request the chariots and receive the prediction, then upon obtaining the chariot they should be "in training" (śaikṣa) as they board the vehicle and depart from the house; if this were the case, then those in training would actually surpass those beyond training (aśaikṣa), because they obtain the chariot within the house.

If you say that those in training (śaikṣa) are not yet called "having obtained the carriage" because you are speaking of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), then why is it that when those beyond training receive their prediction, they are said to "seek the carriage and obtain the carriage," whereas when those in training receive their prediction, they are not so called?
If it is said that because suffering still exists, one cannot speak of "seeking the vehicle" or "bestowing the vehicle," this is also the case for those prior to the seventh stage; reflect upon this.
Question:

Regarding the refutation [of the two vehicles] in the *Śāstra*, it says: "There are no followers of the two vehicles" means there is no nirvāṇa for the two vehicles. Does this mean only that nirvāṇa does not exist, or is it also the case that the practice, the fruit, and so forth do not exist?
Answer:
Some say that when the wisdom that expresses [the truth] realizes the principle that is realized, since there are no two nirvāṇas, it is clear that there are also no two wisdoms;
since the two wisdoms do not exist, there are likewise no two practices.
The teaching arises from the causes of practice, yet there is no separate teaching; therefore, it speaks of "one rain" and so forth.

According to the true meaning, however, it is not thus; rather, there is simply no duality of principle, because it is the one True Suchness, because it is solely Great Nirvāṇa, and because the various preceding and succeeding passages merely state that the Dharmakāya is without differentiation.
Furthermore, how can the essence of the Dharma be considered a single vehicle (ekayāna) in its essence?

The essence of the single vehicle refers to the equal *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* do not possess the essence of that equal *dharmakāya*, because their causal practices and contemplations differ.

Since it has already been stated that "because the practices of cause and effect differ, the practices of clear wisdom and so forth are distinct," and furthermore, as previously stated, "those teachings of the Three Vehicles consist merely of names, phrases, and sentences; they do not possess real meaning, because that real meaning is ineffable."

Furthermore, according to principle, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has a single essence; there are no distinct differences such as variations in the activity of wisdom, because while the reality is one, the skillful means are diverse.
Question:
Since it is said that it is impossible for one who has truly attained arhatship not to have faith in this Dharma, how could there be any impairment or fear?
Answer:

The present statement regarding "actual attainment" is based on those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]. Thus, it is said in the second [section]: "We are now truly the sons of the Buddha," and it is further said: "truly Arhats. This clarifies that those who have not yet turned their minds from suffering are not true sons of the Buddha and are not true Arhats.

Since this is the case for those of indeterminate nature, it is likewise for those of fixed nature; therefore, they are said to "claim for themselves" that they are not truly these two types of noble ones.

If that were so, one would be said to possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*); to claim to have attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state when one has merely attained worldly concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) is called overweening pride; likewise, to have attained only partial liberation while not having attained complete liberation.

Furthermore, although one has not yet attained the Dharma-body, if one claims for oneself that one is equal to the Tathāgata by sitting upon the same bed of liberation, this constitutes pride; even though one lacks afflictions, this is an obstacle to what is known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and thus it is designated as pride despite not obstructing that [liberation].
If it were not thus, there would be no possibility for one who lacked faith at first to be able to believe later;
the same applies to those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), except for those who attain realization after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa during the period of his final transformation.
Although this explanation is offered, it is not as good as the previous interpretation.

In the former case, even if one were to cause harm or experience fear and did not turn their mind [toward the Dharma], they would not slander it upon hearing it, for this accords with the meaning of this text.
Question:

Which sutra states, "I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness"? This sutra originally addresses those who have regressed from bodhicitta; yet, as stated previously, within this assembly there are those like us who, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lifetimes, have already been transformed by the Buddhas.
The second fascicle says:
"I have, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, constantly taught and transformed you all in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas.
Answer:

There are two interpretations: first, it is said that this refers to those who have not yet regressed; specifically regarding those who have newly attained the small [stage], they are said to "not yet have cultivated wholesome roots.

Second, it is said that even if they have previously cultivated the great [stage], because they have not increased them to a superior degree and have not yet established themselves in the fixed position (*niyāma*), they are said to "not yet have cultivated wholesome roots"; this does not mean they have not cultivated them at all.
Question:
Is this based on the present life,
or is it a general teaching concerning many lifetimes?

Answer: This refers generally to many lifetimes; it speaks of those who were transformed by the Buddha across successive ages. How could one say, "I encountered his teaching"? Even if one were transformed by another Buddha, one would still say, "It was for me. This does not pertain solely to this present life. Upon hearing [the Dharma], one immediately attains the realization of a Lesser Fruit (*hīnaphala*); at the very fastest, it takes three lifetimes, as in the case of Śāriputra and others, who required sixty *kalpas*. How could it be that the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle was established for the first time in this life alone?
If that is so, why does the second fascicle state that upon first hearing the Buddha's Dharma, one immediately believes and accepts it?
Answer:
The phrase "first hearing" is also used as a general expression; it does not necessarily refer to the present moment.

If that is so, why did it say: "In the past, I was attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins; the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodox views and preached nirvāṇa"?
Answer:
This is stated based on this present life; it does not mean that one attains awakening merely upon hearing [the teaching] in this lifetime.
Another explanation states that this is based on the perspective of those who undergo transformation; in reality, it is not so.
When I say "observing with the Buddha-eye," it means observing with the five eyes of a Buddha.
These five eyes shall be briefly analyzed by way of five categories:

This consists of five parts: first, establishing the essential nature; second, explaining the name; third, identifying the person who attains it; fourth, the establishment and rejection [of categories];

and fifth, the mutual inclusion of characteristics. Regarding the first, establishing the essential nature: the various schools offer differing explanations concerning the fleshly eye and the divine eye, as has been extensively analyzed elsewhere; for fear of prolixity, they shall not be recounted here in full.
However, according to what is taught in our own Mahāyāna school, there are those who designate the seeds of visual consciousness as "the eye. Thus, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves appearing as the aspect of an object; in order to establish the internal and external bases, the Buddha spoke of these ten."
There are those who maintain that the species of form is called the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states:

"The functional capacity for form within consciousness is called the five faculties; it is logical that this capacity and the objective form have served as mutual conditions for one another since beginningless time."
Some say that the karmic seeds capable of producing the visual faculty are themselves called the "visual faculty. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In order to avoid the aforementioned faults and difficulties, some clarify their adherence to that [previous] position and further offer this defense:
'The karmic seeds within consciousness are what are termed the five material faculties.'"
The three preceding explanations are all incorrect.

The *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Pañcaskandhaka*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and other treatises state that the essential nature of the fleshly eye consists of the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which functions as the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Regarding this, there are three [subsequent] explanations:
One view holds that it is the seed, another that it is the active manifestation, and yet another that it pertains to both; this last explanation is considered correct.
Thus, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* asks:
"What is the eye-faculty?"

This refers to that which is derived from the four great elements and serves as the basis for visual consciousness; because it takes visible form as its object, it comprises both the seeds and the manifest state.

As for the essential nature of the divine eye faculty (*divyacakṣur-indriya*), it consists of pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*); this is because it is the result of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga’s *Prajñā-śāstra* states:
"Because they are subsumed under form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, there are two types of subsumption under form:
namely, the fruit of the Dharma (*dharma-phala*) and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*)."
The Dharma-fruit is precisely flesh, and the cultivation-fruit is precisely heaven.
"Dharma" is a general term referring to the karma that can induce [rebirth];
"flesh" is the fruit of this [karma].
Although it is known that the general term applies [to all], the term "flesh" (māṃsa) alone is used here, just as when one speaks of the "sense-base of form" (rūpāyatana).
"Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to meditative concentration (samādhi); that which arises from the cause of cultivation is called the "fruit of cultivation.

Regarding the two types of eyes of those who follow the foolish dharmas, both have wisdom (prajñā) as their nature, because they differ in that one takes the ultimate truth (paramārtha) as its object and the other takes the conventional truth (saṃvṛti) as its object.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga’s *Prajñā-śāstra* states:
"It is comprised within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Furthermore, because of the power of the wisdom of the ultimate meaning, and because conventional wisdom functions without inversion, these are two aspects of a single wisdom distinguished according to their respective objects and functions. The Buddha-eye has the preceding four eyes as its nature; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

For example, just as the four rivers that flow into the ocean are collectively called "the waters of heaven and earth," so too the previous four eyes within the Buddha’s body are termed the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*).

According to the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* by the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, however, it is the Buddha’s subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that is named the Buddha-eye; the treatise states that this is comprised of all modes of cognition and all appropriate wisdoms.

Furthermore, it is said that among all types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the effortless wisdom regarding all aspects (*sarvākārānābhogajñāna*) is designated as the Buddha-eye. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this by establishing its essence based on the general [definition], whereas the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* establishes its essence according to each specific [category].

Furthermore, in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the first four [eyes] are based on the cause, while the Buddha-eye is defined in terms of the fruit. Otherwise, how could the fruit of Buddhahood possess an eye-faculty that is a maturation produced by karma?
Furthermore, how could the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Buddha not be non-erroneous by virtue of its fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*), since it arises spontaneously?
Alternatively, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna*, these are collectively termed the "Buddha-eye"; because their wisdom is predominant, they are collectively designated as "wisdom."
If that is so, why is it said that "in all modes, there is the wisdom of effortless cognition in all modes"?
Based on this, it follows that the term "Buddha-eye" refers specifically to the subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Therefore, the former interpretation is superior.
Second, regarding the explanation of the name, there are two parts: first, the general; second, the specific.

As for the general name "eye" (*cakṣus*), in the Sanskrit language it is called *pañcacakṣu*. *Pañca* here means "five," and *cakṣu* means "exhaustion of activity. This signifies that, like the practice of precepts, it is able to see all various things to their ultimate end; thus it is called "exhaustion of activity."

The term "eye" (*cakṣus*) is used here as a secondary translation and is not the primary one; in the Sanskrit language, it is called *cakṣus*, which carries the meaning of "that which illuminates and gazes.
The word "five" (*pañca*) is a numeral, and this is an analysis based on its numerical value.

To explain the individual names: "flesh" refers to the matter that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma; since this flesh is the eye, it is named by means of a *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound. "Deva" (heavenly being) refers to the divine function of sovereign brilliance and purity;

although the name "deva" applies generally to the Desire, Form, and Formless realms, here it specifically denotes a deva of the Form Realm. Because it is the eye of such a deva, it is designated by a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Alternatively, "deva" refers to the brilliance and purity that is the very fruit of meditative concentration; since this deva is the eye itself, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

This explanation is subject to ambiguity and furthermore contradicts the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. That treatise states that because the gods possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is not identical to the [physical] eye; rather, the clear illumination [of objects] is called wisdom (*prajñā*), and wisdom is itself the eye—this is also a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Dharma is the object; the eye that takes Dharma as its condition is called the "Dharma-eye. Although wisdom and other [faculties] that take [Dharma] as their condition are collectively termed "Dharma," while others each take specific objects individually, this [Dharma-eye] is able to take them universally.
Furthermore, because it takes the teachings as its object, this alone is called the "Dharma-eye" (*dharma-cakṣus*).
The term "Buddha" is as explained previously; the "eye of the Buddha" is called the "Buddha-eye" (*buddha-cakṣus*), following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis.

Regarding the third point, those who attain [the divine eye]: among sentient beings within the two realms of desire and form, if they possess the fundamental dhyānas of the four concentrations—whether they belong to the six heavens of the desire realm or to the three continents (excluding Uttarakuru)—they are able to produce the divine eye, for it is admitted that they have attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The followers of the Two Vehicles possess the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), because it illuminates the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Although they also attain the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), it is not said that they achieve it because it is inferior due to its smallness.
Bodhisattvas possess the dharma-eye; because they have the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākāra-jñatā*), they are able to take all things as their objects.
The Buddha possesses the Buddha-eye, which is manifest and can be known through its marks.

Furthermore, in the process of accomplishment, each subsequent stage necessarily entails the attainment of all preceding stages; thus, while the superior includes the inferior, the inferior does not entail the subsequent. Therefore, although one accomplishes the preceding stages, it is not necessarily the case that one will accomplish the subsequent ones.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Devas possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); those of the Two Vehicles possess the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*); and Bodhisattvas possess the dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
Question:
If the Buddha possesses the Dharma-eye, it is designated as the Buddha-eye; if a Bodhisattva possesses the Dharma-eye, should it not be called the Bodhisattva-eye?
Answer:
The Buddha-eye exists only for the Buddha, and its name is established in accordance with the Buddha.
The Dharma is not exclusively for Bodhisattvas; it is called the "Dharma-eye" (dharmacakṣus) based on its object. The same principle applies to others.
Question:

If the Dharma is not exclusive to Bodhisattvas and is therefore not called the "Bodhisattva-eye," why is it that the divine eye (divyacakṣus), which is not exclusive to devas, is nevertheless called the "deva-eye"?

Furthermore, if the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is not possessed by gods alone yet is still called the "divine eye," then why should the fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus), which is not possessed by humans alone, not be called the "human eye"?
Answer:

The fleshly eye is a retribution common to other realms of existence and is therefore not called the "exclusive human eye. The divine eye belongs exclusively to that [divine] state; for this reason, it is called the "divine eye."
Question:

Since the dharma [of vision] exists in the Buddha, it is not called the "Bodhisattva eye"; yet since the celestial [nature] is accomplished by all classes of beings, why is it exclusively termed "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*)?
Answer:

The Buddhas and others also bear the title of "deva" (heavenly being); because they possess this universally, it is called the "divine eye. Although humans may give rise to such a faculty, as it belongs to the category of the heavens, it is termed the "divine eye.

Furthermore, names are merely provisional designations; why then seek their meaning with such hardship? Even if one were to establish many such designations, there would ultimately be difficulties; for now, let us each establish these names according to their respective meanings.
Regarding the fourth point on establishment and exclusion: Why are exactly five eyes established, neither more nor less?
Answer:
All dharmas, in brief, are of two kinds:
There are two types: first, material phenomena (rūpadharma); second, non-material phenomena (arūpadharma). Within material phenomena, there are two kinds:
first, manifest and proximate matter; second, concealed and remote matter.
The fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is established because it perceives manifest and proximate forms; the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is established because it perceives hidden and distant forms.

Alternatively, among the sense organs, there is a distinction between the results of concentration and distraction: the eye that is the result of distracted karma is established as the internal eye, while the eye produced by meditative concentration is established as the divine eye; these two types are distinguished because they differ in terms of superiority and inferiority.
Therefore, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states:
"The fruit of the Dharma and the fruit of cultivation—these constitute the five eyes.

Because they take coarse objects as their domain, they are subsumed under the first [eye], the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Within non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), there are both objective principles (*li*) and objective facts (*shi*). To realize the objective principles, the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is established; to realize the objective facts, the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) is established.

Furthermore, although it is a single wisdom, because the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms differ, it is established as two; thus, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* categorizes them as being subsumed under ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Moreover, by correlating the fruit with the cause, the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) is established as a general term; therefore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the four eyes prior [to Buddhahood] are collectively termed the Buddha-eye upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood.
Alternatively, based on the individuals [who attained them], there are five types; one may understand this by reflecting upon it.
Although such is the case regarding their abolition or establishment, what is their sequence?
Answer:
According to the sequence of their arising based on inferiority and superiority, among the various forms, the fleshly eye is the most inferior, perceiving only what is manifest;
the divine eye is superior to it, perceiving both the hidden and the manifest; therefore, it is mentioned immediately after the fleshly eye.

Regarding non-form phenomena, conventional wisdom that realizes conventional truth is not analogous [to the preceding cases]; furthermore, because the realization of the conventional arises from the realization of the ultimate, it is said to be "subsequent. Since wisdom comes first and the dharma comes later, and because cause precedes effect, it follows the Buddha-eye.
Therefore, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states:
"These constitute the five eyes; because they are coarse objects, they are the first form.
Based on the power of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), worldly knowledge functions without inversion; therefore, the inclusion of the ultimate truth is placed first."

Regarding the inclusion of the five aspects: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are three types of eyes, whereas in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are ten. The listing of their names and the manner of their mutual inclusion are all as explained in the commentaries.

If one were to correlate the eleven [categories] established in the third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* with these, it would be too cumbersome to describe them here; those who wish to explore this in detail should consult that text.
Question:

The Sūtra states that when Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, "the net of their doubts is entirely removed," and that "all twelve hundred Arhats shall likewise become Buddhas. Of the two types of doubt held by the Bodhisattvas, which one is being removed now?
Answer:
Both are excluded.
One knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha, and one does not doubt that others cannot become Buddhas.
How is this known?
Answer:

It is because in the third section of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Treatise), in order to refute the attachment to seeking exclusively the Mahāyāna while denying the existence of the two vehicles, two analogies are presented.
Question:
Since a bodhisattva knows that they will attain Buddhahood, why is there no bestowal of a prophecy (vyākaraṇa)?
Answer:

The śrāvakas have long studied the Lesser Vehicle; although they believe that they themselves can attain Buddhahood, they may not yet possess certainty. To cause them to attain a mind of certainty, the Buddha grants them the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

Bodhisattvas have not previously studied the Hīnayāna; however, fearing that they might regress, when they hear the teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), they realize there is no separate Hīnayāna and immediately abide in the certainty of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, they do not require formal prediction (vyākaraṇa).
Furthermore, he also granted them individual predictions.
Since it was previously stated that "not one will fail to become a Buddha," this was a prediction given collectively; why, then, were they not predicted individually?
Answer:
Because it is concise and because it is appropriate for those who hear this distinct teaching.
Question:
Since it is said that all twelve hundred arhats shall likewise become buddhas, do they know for themselves that they will become buddhas, or do they not?

If they had known this for themselves, the twelve hundred people should have received their prediction simultaneously with Śāriputra; why, then, did you say that it was only after the parable of the conjured city that they gave rise to the mind of understanding and were finally granted their prediction?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.

One says that [the disciples] know they have attained [the goal], but have not yet proceeded toward it because their joy is slight; only upon hearing the teaching of the "transformed city" do they understand how to abandon the small vehicle, and only then are they granted the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

The second group said they did not yet know; they had merely heard that the Buddha would declare them to become Buddhas, and it was only upon hearing the third turning of the wheel that they finally attained realization.
Question:

Why is it that when Bodhisattvas hear [the teaching], their doubts are immediately removed and they know they will become Buddhas, whereas these twelve hundred people could not know for themselves that it was merely the Buddha’s declaration?
Answer: This is because of the difference between sharp and dull faculties.

Śāriputra, possessing sharp faculties, understood upon hearing it once; the Bodhisattvas, being even more superior, had their doubts removed immediately. As for the twelve hundred [disciples], their faculties were dull, and thus they were not yet able to understand.
Question:

According to the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits," it is stated that if one hears even a single chapter on the "Life Span" and its merits, it is impossible for that person to ever regress from a single aspect of enlightenment.
Śāriputra and others had previously heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at such assemblies as that of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; for what reason did they all subsequently recede?
Answer: There are two explanations.
First, it is said that there is no possibility of ultimate regression, because even if one regresses, they will eventually arouse [the resolve] again.

Second, it is said that this refers to those who possess superior benefit, or alternatively, it refers to those who have attained realization; thus, the nine purities are explained. The third fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

first, purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), which means abiding well in ethical discipline and perceiving even the slightest transgression as a source of great fear while training in the precepts.
Second is purity of mind, which, by relying on purity of ethical discipline, leads to abiding in the four dhyānas.
Third is purity of view, which, by relying on purity of mind, results in the realization of the truths through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

Fourth is the purification through the overcoming of doubt (*kāṅkṣā-vitaraṇa-viśuddhi*); based on the purification through vision (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*), one is without confusion or doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.

Fifth is the purification through the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*mārgāmārgajñānadarśana-viśuddhi*); based on the purification through the overcoming of doubt, one attains sublime knowledge and vision, knowing that the path taught by the Buddha is capable of leading to deliverance, whereas that taught by non-Buddhist teachers cannot bring an end to suffering.

The purification of vision through knowledge of the six modes of practice, and the purification of vision through knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path, also attain the sublime purification of vision through knowledge. Regarding the paths of deliverance, there are superior, middling, and inferior levels, namely those comprised within the "difficult progress with sluggish intuition" and so forth.

Regarding the purification of knowledge and vision through the abandonment of the seven types of conduct: by relying on the purification of knowledge and vision regarding conduct, one attains sublime wisdom, namely, the realization that "I should abandon the lower-middle types of conduct and initiate the higher, sublime noble conduct."

Eighth is the purity of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa-śuddhi*): by relying on the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of conduct, one realizes the state without remainder, wherein all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted.

Ninth is the purity of the buddha-field (*kṣetra-śuddhi*): this refers to the unsurpassed vessel of merit shared by all Buddhas, which manifests inconceivable adornments of the buddha-field, including the utterly pure thought of a Buddha, the utterly pure thought of a bodhisattva, and the thoughts of their retinues.
Question:

In the Parable of the Burning House, Śāriputra requested [the teaching], and the twelve hundred people immediately became those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Why, then, does the commentary explain that it was for the sake of sentient beings who are still in training (śaikṣa) and possess the nature of afflictions?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.

One says: the discussion of the fundamental refers to the provisional, where the "fundamental" refers to ordinary beings; now, by using a metaphor to clarify this, it is said that they possess a nature of full afflictions. Since this speaks of the former intention, there is no contradiction.

The second [interpretation] states that, based on the request of the śrāvakas, this is primarily for those beyond training (aśaikṣa) while incidentally preparing for those still in training (śaikṣa); however, since it refers to "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana) incidentally, and the text regarding those beyond training is explicit, the treatise omits further explanation of it.

This is not so; for the core tenet of this sūtra is to clarify the One Vehicle (ekayāna). How could it be otherwise when the "Herbs Chapter" speaks of various vehicles to allow beings to know their differences? This is clearly understood from the text as being directed toward internal śrāvakas still in training, urging them toward the Great Vehicle; therefore, I have not cited it in full.
Question:
Regarding the vehicles of the sheep and the deer, what phenomena do they actually refer to?
Answer:

According to the commentary of the masters, they take the mundane meditative mind (*laukika-samādhi-citta*) that follows the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the two vehicles’ state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). They point to this [mind] as the "chariot of the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) that leads the child out; however, because this mundane mind cannot actually comprehend all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), the child cannot exit once the door is opened.
This can be cultivated for a brief moment; in meaning, it refers to "seeking the vehicle.

Therefore, the Treatise says: "The first kind of person is granted various worldly roots of goodness, samādhis, and merits so that they may sport in them, and is subsequently led to enter Great Nirvāṇa."

If that is so, why does the subsequent analogy state that one "rides these three vehicles and amuses oneself with the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, and so forth"?
Answer:
Because those are the ornaments of this vehicle.
Furthermore, all phenomena within the untainted body are also called "untainted.
If that were so, then an ox-cart should also be like this.
Answer:
Because that [state] is ultimate and possesses real virtue;
whereas this [state] is a mere empty indication and is not ultimate.
If that were so, could that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) be called "leaving the house"?
Answer:
It is called "leaving the house" because one emerges from the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the untainted knowledge of arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) attained at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) is designated as the sheep and deer carts; this is because the subsequent passage speaks of mastery, being unbound, having nothing to rely upon or seek, and so forth, regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and other qualities.
If that is so, how is it that they leave the gate to seek a vehicle?
It is because they have already attained such knowledge. Answer:

This wisdom is provisionally designated as "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā); however, because it cannot comprehend all phenomena and must be further cultivated, it is figuratively called "seeking the vehicle.
If this is so, how can it be termed "worldly"?
Answer:
It is called "worldly" because it takes conventional things as its object and because it employs inferior wisdom.

If that is so, then when speaking of a city in contrast to a chariot, one should take the ultimate truth; why then does the treatise refer to "the city of Nirvāṇa" as the city of the various dhyānas and samādhis? Since Nirvāṇa is already identified with the city of dhyāna and samādhi, for what reason is bodhi identified with the subsequent worldly wisdom?

Furthermore, the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the two vehicles cannot give rise to the comprehensive knowledge that understands all phenomena; how, then, could it be said to "cause them to play"?
Therefore, what was previously stated is correct.
Question:
Question: Do those who seek the vehicle outside the gate represent all three vehicles, or do they all exclusively seek the two vehicles?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.

First, it is said that the cord pertains to all three vehicles (*yāna*), because the text contains no distinction [between them], because the masters of old have so explained it, and because it speaks of "all sons.
Second, it is said that the cord pertains only to the two vehicles (*yāna*) and not to Bodhisattvas; why is this?
The house is a metaphor for the realm of分段 (duḥkha-saṃsāra). To emerge from this realm is called "leaving the house.

The two vehicles leave the house upon attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*); the Bodhisattva leaves the house at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Since those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning have not yet attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), their capacity to cultivate and learn toward its attainment is called "seeking the carriage."
From the first bhūmi upward, because one has obtained the vehicle of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), there is no need to seek it;
however, if one considers the act of cultivation and study itself as "seeking the vehicle," then since this cultivation occurs throughout all ten bhūmis, one is constantly seeking it.
If that were so, then there would be no Bodhisattva who does not mount a carriage; how then could it be said that "some ride in carriages and play"? Furthermore, the treatise states:

"In order to cause [beings] to enter the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), he manifests the bestowing of immeasurable wisdom-activity (*jñāna-karman*). Since those from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward already possess wisdom-activity, although they know how to practice and study, the sutra does not say they "seek" [the vehicle], but speaks of them "playing.

As for the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), they have not yet emerged from the house nor attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); since they have not yet reached the first stage, their ability to practice and study is figuratively termed "seeking the carriage."

Furthermore, the treatise states: "The first type of person causes them to sport in various worldly roots of goodness, samādhis, and merits, and subsequently leads them into the city of Great Nirvāṇa. Because they are given the mundane goodness of humans and devas, they have not yet attained the Truth and thus must be said to 'seek' it;
the Bodhisattva does not point toward the sheep or the deer. From the First Ground upward, one attains the Truth; therefore, the Bodhisattva does not seek."
Some say that because those of initial capacity point toward the empty, they must seek the cart.
Others say that while three gates are heard within the house, only one is seen outside; not knowing who knows that one, they must therefore seek it, and so forth.
All these are not literal statements.
Question:
Since the Bodhisattvas do not seek a vehicle, can they be said to have "left the house" and be "seated"?
Answer:

It is said that he "exits the house and sits" because, for those of the Two Vehicles, their training is ultimate, their obstructions are exhausted, their minds are stilled, and they have established the fruit;

whereas for Bodhisattvas, their training is not yet ultimate, they have not yet exhausted all obstructions, they do not establish a final fruit, and their minds are not yet stilled, so it cannot be said that they "sit in the open air."
If one were to argue that even those who have attained the first three fruits are also called "sitting in the open," then those still in training (*śaikṣa*) would likewise be so designated.

If you claim that those in training are also called "those who sit outside," why does the subsequent analogy state: "By the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, they emerge from the perilous path of the terrors and sufferings of the triple world and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa"?

Furthermore, it is explained that a Bodhisattva may also be said to be "seated. Although they do not yet abide in cessation nor have they fully mastered the fruit [of Arhatship], they are nonetheless termed "seated" because they dwell securely in wisdom; for they are able to subdue the afflictions and transcend the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*), thus being called one who has emerged from the triple world into the open space where there is no obstruction.
If this were so, then the three fruits [of the Śrāvaka path] would also be like this; even if this were granted, there would be no fault, as one may freely choose what to adopt or reject.
Question:

Regarding the three vehicles, outside their gates there are many differences in the nature of these vehicles. According to ancient interpretations, they are *nirvāṇa*; according to the present explanation, they refer to the subsequently attained correct wisdom (*prsthalabdha-samyagjñāna*).
Taking *nirvāṇa* as the body of the chariot is clearly stated in the sūtras and śāstras.
The sūtra states in full: "Desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek *nirvāṇa* for oneself is like those sons seeking the sheep-chariots to exit the burning house."
The treatise states that they enter nirvana later; therefore, it takes the subsequent wisdom as the three vehicles. What textual evidence is there for this?
Answer:
There is clear evidence in both the sutras and the treatises.

The sheep and deer are said to represent subsequent wisdom; the treatise states that "the first person" refers to one who is made to sport through the skillful means of various worldly roots of goodness, samādhis, and merits, and is subsequently led into nirvāṇa.
Since it speaks of "various roots of goodness" and "the merits of samādhi," it is clear that this is not *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the description of the ox-cart, it says they "seek all-knowledge, Buddha-knowledge, self-existent knowledge, and teacherless knowledge," as well as the Tathāgata’s "knowledge and vision, compassion, and thoughts of peace and happiness"; thus, it is clear that this is not *nirvāṇa*.
Question:
Regarding the textual passage concerning the city, how should one determine the correct reading?
Answer:
Taking wisdom as the correct [standard].
If this is so, how should the preceding passage be interpreted?
Answer:
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it possesses the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, because one seeks the [deer or antelope] as *nirvāṇa*, one does not conflate *nirvāṇa* with the deer or antelope.

If that is so, others also explain that it is called "knowledge and vision" and so forth because it is the nature of knowledge and vision, and because it is the nature of samādhi; in reality, this is indeed *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, what is the discrepancy here?
The answer is:
because it contradicts many scriptural passages.
Regarding the description of the deer-drawn carriage, it says: "He delights in solitary tranquility and deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena.

Regarding the ox-drawn carriage, it says: "Out of compassion, he brings peace and happiness to deliver gods and humans," and further says: "I myself take delight in the untainted faculties, powers, and so forth," and again says: "I possess such great carriages made of the seven treasures, numbering in the infinite; I ought to give them equally to each with an impartial mind, and it is not fitting to make distinctions."
If it is nirvana, how can you say there are "innumerable" [instances] and that each is given?

If you argue that although True Suchness (*tathatā*) is one, yet when speaking of the seven kinds or ten suchnesses and so forth, these are said to be "immeasurable" and "each distinct" based on the means of realization (*pramāṇa*), what fault is there in this?
Otherwise, if one explains that wisdom is the chariot and principle is the treasure-trove, what contradiction would there be?

To speak of them collectively as "principle" would result in a deficiency regarding bodhi if one were to grasp only principle; now, by grasping wisdom, it is explained that both wisdom and abandonment are fully present.

Furthermore, the first [verse] previously stated that one ultimately causes [beings] to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); moreover, the treatise states that one causes them to enter the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), and also because it bestows immeasurable wisdom-activity (*jñāna-karman*).

Furthermore, a sutra states: "The dharmas thus attained are adorned by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom"; it also says, "The lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions"; it further says, "Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)"; it also says, "Riding this precious chariot, one travels through the four quarters"; and it speaks of various meritorious qualities such as the faculties and powers.

Furthermore, it is said: "I have now fashioned this chariot for you. Therefore, the analogy of the treasure place refers to that which exists primordially and is not created; it concerns conditioned phenomena produced through cultivation, which are described using terms such as "fashioning," and cannot be called a conjured city.
Although it is also said that the principle (li) performs action, it merely bears the name "action" because it lacks substantial reality.

The ox-cart is the same in this regard; the son should abandon it. If one adopts the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not said to perform action, as there are many proofs for this, which I shall not cite in full for fear of prolixity. Therefore, the jewel is used as a metaphor for the principle, while the cart is a metaphor for the superior wisdom.
Question:

The parable of the impoverished son serves as an antidote to those with one-sided overweening pride (*adhimāna*). It states that my vehicle and the Tathāgata’s vehicle are equal and without distinction. If one says that my vehicle and the Tathāgata’s vehicle are without distinction, this refers to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of a Tathāgata; it is precisely the meaning taught in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding śrāvakas becoming Buddhas and attaining identity with the Buddha through their own intrinsic aspiration (*āśaya*).
What need is there for an antidote?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.

One interpretation holds that it is permitted [to say] one is equal to the Tathāgata from the perspective of the Hīnayāna; this is taught as a remedy for the "poor son" analogy. However, when one thinks, "I am equal to the Buddha," and thus attains this very aspiration, it is no longer a remedial teaching.

One interpretation states that because those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) do not cultivate the path to becoming a Buddha, they are merely enabled to attain the mental disposition of sameness (samatā-āśaya);

whereas those of unfixed nature (aniyata-gotra) are destined to become Buddhas and are permitted to be equal to them—it is said [that the teaching] is for the purpose of preventing those with obstacles from turning their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
There is no contradiction, as their respective antidotes and intended purposes differ.
Question:

Since the four great śrāvakas attained realization through the parables and were thereby established as those beyond training (aśaikṣa), why does the treatise state that these were spoken for the sake of those still in training (śaikṣa)?
Answer:
It is like the former state of being deluded and attached while still in the causal stage; now having attained awakening, it is likened to the "learner" (śaikṣa) of the past.
Furthermore, since one has personally understood, explaining this to enlighten others by calling them "learners"—what fault could there be in that?
Not so; for how could these four persons be their own antidotes?
Question:
Is the prophecy for śrāvakas intended as a general indetermination, or are there others as well?
Answer:

According to the explanation in the treatise, these apply to both those of indeterminate lineage and those who manifest through transformation; thus the treatise states that there are two kinds of śrāvakas for whom the Tathāgata bestows a prediction: namely, the śrāvakas who are emanations, and those who, having regressed, subsequently resolve their minds toward bodhicitta.
Question:
Who is the one who is indeterminate?
Who is the one who undergoes transformation?
Answer:

The treatise does not provide a definitive judgment; however, according to the sūtra text, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra alone is said to be a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the others are mostly indeterminate, as it is stated that they all previously generated the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
Question:

If it is granted that there are actual śrāvakas who can turn their minds toward Buddhahood, why does the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* state, "We śrāvakas are like withered seeds, no longer of any use"? Furthermore, both the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* and the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra* do not permit this.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are real śrāvakas because they are all transformations;
this is just as it is not necessarily the case that seeds do not sprout—therefore, there is no doubt regarding this meaning.
If they will not undergo further rebirth, how can they practice for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
Answer:

All of these are based on praising the excellence of the Mahāyāna so as to discourage those of the Hīnayāna from seeking [liberation] through that path; furthermore, because those of indeterminate nature will ultimately return to the Great Vehicle, and so that those with the Mahāyāna nature may swiftly proceed toward the Great.
This is not so; how could the sūtras and śāstras possibly contradict one another?

According to these various texts, at the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, all four types of śrāvakas were initially present in the gathering. After the three instances of the Buddha’s refusal to preach, those of superior capacity withdrew from their seats. This is because it is not said that the true noble ones also withdrew from their seats, as the hearing of this sūtra causes them to become non-deluded regarding the Dharma.

In the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, it is stated that [certain beings] were not granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and were not obstructed from remaining in their seats; alternatively, they may lack a fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). The *Śāstra* says: "Because there would be harm and fear, because no prediction was given, and because their faculties (*indriya*) were not yet matured, they did not remain in their seats. Thus, one may choose to include or exclude them as one pleases.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the conjured city?
Answer:
As explained in the Commentary (*śāstra*), a supplementary explanation states:

"The mundane samādhi of the final mind of an Arhat is called a 'transformed city' (*pariṇāmika-nagara*), just like the substance of the two carts. This is because the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) does not form a conceptual understanding [of it as such], whereas the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) forms the conceptual understanding of it as *nirvāṇa* and takes it to be ultimate; thus, the Sūtra has transformed it."
The treatise states: "As for the fourth person, it is because they employ skillful means to cause entry into the city of nirvāṇa;
the city of nirvāṇa is the city of the various dhyānas and samādhis.
If this is so, how can they bring an end to all sufferings?
Answer:
Because they have abandoned obstacles and because they have emerged from the three realms, it is like two chariots.
Since they have already attained what is called "leaving the house," why can this [state] not bring an end to suffering?
If that is so, why is it that the two carts cannot be obtained,
while the aforementioned illusory city is said to be entered?
Answer:
Because they cannot fully comprehend all phenomena and because it is not the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), they do not obtain the vehicle. Why is this?
Because they have not yet abandoned the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), how could they obtain the conjured city?
Because the suffering of the three realms has ceased, because liberation has been attained, and because the obstacles of affliction have already been abandoned.
If that is so, how is it called *nirvāṇa*?
Answer:
Because it is a provisional designation for nirvana.
The second [type] says that merely being free from delusion is called liberation, yet in reality one has not attained complete liberation.

It further states: "At that time, the mind thinks to itself that it has attained nirvana; this is like those with overweening pride who claim to have attained the fruit when they have not actually attained it—this case is also like that."
If that is so, would it not follow that those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not possess the "remainder"?
Answer:
Just as their untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) remains hidden and unmanifested, one speaks only of worldly knowledge (laukika-jñāna), which is termed the "chariot."
This case is also like that;

although there are remaining [defilements], because they are not ultimate, they are concealed and not made manifest, so as to cause one to grasp the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, the treatise says: "to cause entry into the city of Nirvāṇa.
As for the city of Nirvāṇa, it is the city of all dhyānas and samādhis.
If it were simply referring to that which remains,
why would it be called the "city of the various dhyānas and samādhis"?
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also says:
Regarding the attainment of the four knowledges and nirvāṇa: this indicates that one is close to the realm of nirvāṇa, clarifying that it is not actual nirvāṇa because it is said to be "near.
If it were actual nirvāṇa, one would say it has already been attained; why then would it be called "near"?
The tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Regarding the statement that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not possess nirvāṇa, there are two interpretations.

The first says: 'Alternatively, this refers to those of indeterminate lineage who, having attained the state of one beyond training, immediately turn toward the Great Vehicle; it is said that they do not attain [nirvāṇa] because their attainment is identical to that of this [indeterminate lineage].'"

If one is a person of fixed nature, the two vehicles—the sheep and the deer—give rise to wisdom within them; the aforementioned "transformed city" represents the two types of nirvana. This is because for such a person it is ultimate and not merely a temporary rest, and because they do not proceed toward the Great Vehicle; thus, they differ from those of indeterminate nature.
Question:

Just as the three carts were sought out to provide an incentive, the parable of the burning house was taught to engender revulsion and prevent further seeking; yet, the three carts were separately explained as an antidote. Since there are those of fixed nature who, though in reality there is no nirvāṇa, possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and because they possess worldly *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa where in reality there is none—this is the parable of the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) taught as an antidote for them.
It should be understood that since those still in training (śaikṣa) grasp worldly samādhi as nirvāṇa, yet it is in reality not nirvāṇa, this is called "overweening pride" (adhimāna).

Now, it is precisely for their sake that worldly samādhi is described as a "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura); it should be viewed like the burning house, so that they will grow weary of it and not take hold of it. How then can it be said that the fourth person was led into the city of nirvāṇa through skillful means? [This would contradict the fact that worldly samādhi is merely a provisional device.]
If grasping at worldly samādhi were called *nirvāṇa*, would this not increase that very attachment?

Furthermore, you do not understand that the request to enter that city was an emanation; since it was said to be an emanation, why strive so diligently for the sake of later attaining the Great Vehicle?
Answer:

It is precisely for the sake of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that their past deeds are recounted, so as to provisionally allow them rest; seeking temporary repose, they are led toward the Great Vehicle from the state of emptiness. Now, further meanings are presented to counteract those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Those who are not yet fixed are capable of turning toward the Great Vehicle, whereas those who are fixed cling to the nirvāṇa attained by those beyond training, regarding it as ultimate and directing their minds with joy toward it.

Now the Buddha explains that what they [perceived] was not a real extinction, but was like a conjured city. The reason he previously spoke of it as *nirvāṇa* was my skillful means to cause them to turn back; I had them enter this provisional city of *nirvāṇa* so they might rest from their exhaustion. Once they have passed beyond this city, I lead them into the city of Great *Nirvāṇa*, the place of precious jewels. Thus, to cause those in training (*śaikṣa*) to know how to abandon this and seek the Great, I spoke of the conjured city as an antidote.

This serves as an antidote; it is not that the fourth person mentioned here says that having created the conjured city, one should then seek to enter it further. It should be explained according to the text, which does not contradict reason.
My ignorance being thus, I further hope for an excellent explanation.
Question:
For what purpose were the ten unsurpassed [teachings] spoken?
Answer:

This is specifically for those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage. Therefore, the treatise states that the rain analogy is taught because it demonstrates the unsurpassed seed-nature; the phrase "that which you practice is the bodhisattva path" refers to those who, having once regressed from generating the bodhicitta, generate it again, such that the roots of goodness previously cultivated are not extinguished and they attain the same fruit as those [bodhisattvas] who did not regress.

The intended meaning is that within the bodies of those of the two vehicles there exist the seeds of bodhisattvas; thus, by cultivating them again, they are all able to become Buddhas. This is so that those who have already resolved their minds may make it firm, and those who have not yet resolved their minds may hear of the Unsurpassed [Vehicle] and likewise resolve their minds.

Since it is said that after having regressed one may again resolve to attain enlightenment, and that the roots of goodness previously cultivated are not extinguished because they will likewise result in the attainment of the fruit later on, this demonstrates that [the stages] are indeterminate.
If this is so, why are the ten kinds of unsurpassed [stages] not all included within the main body of the teaching?
Answer:

It is not solely for the purpose of revealing the principle of the One Vehicle; it also serves to praise and encourage its upholding. Therefore, it encompasses both parts; I shall briefly outline the general framework, without elaborating on the remaining details.
Question:
What is the sequential order of these ten unsurpassed [qualities]?
Answer:

Inferring from this meaning, it is intended to encourage the arousal of the bodhicitta by relying on the power of causes; it describes how they have previously planted great causes so that they may practice accordingly and attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, it speaks of the "unsurpassed seed," which clearly explains that the wholesome bodhisattva path you are practicing is indeed such, and clarifies that the roots of goodness from your past arousal of the mind are not extinguished.
Now, hearing the Buddha-dharma serves as the cause for attaining the fruit later;

since there is this superior cause, one must cultivate the unsurpassed cause over a long period of time before being able to attain the fruit. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was nearly attaining Bodhi after ten kalpas had passed, thereby demonstrating that because the fruit is supreme, one must cultivate the unsurpassed cause.
Next, the unsurpassed practice is explained. Regarding the unsurpassed practice, one must necessarily perform the Great Practice; why then would it be bestowed as something small in the interim?

It is simply because, although they had previously resolved upon the Great Mind, they were unable to suddenly generate that Greatness during the intermediate stage. Thus, as a provisional skillful means, their suffering was first stilled, after which they were led forward toward the Great. Therefore, it is said that the power of increasing merit is unsurpassed.
How is it known that they once resolved their minds on the Great Vehicle in the past?
It is because the parable of the tied jewel was taught to lead them to realization; thus, the subsequent teaching is intended to bring about understanding of the Unsurpassed.
Since it is known that they cultivated the great causes for a long time in the past, yet withdrew midway merely out of fear of the Great Vehicle;
Now, being able to recollect, comprehend, and practice, one shall attain a pure land just as all bodhisattvas do; therefore, the Pure Land is explained next.
Since unsurpassed comprehension has been further enhanced, one is capable of hearing the teaching of liberation; therefore, the Unsurpassed is explained next.

Having heard the unsurpassed teaching and accumulated causes through practice over many kalpas, all have become superior persons; therefore, next, the teaching and transformation of sentient beings is explained.

Since the unsurpassed and supreme causes have been accumulated, one shall attain the supreme fruit, which differs from that of the two vehicles; therefore, next, the attainment of the supreme fruit of great bodhi is explained.

Although he has realized extinction (*nirvāṇa*), he is able to manifest his body to benefit sentient beings; while the Dharma-body and Reward-body remain eternally present, the Transformation-body adapts to conditions without fixed form. Thus, though extinguished it is not extinguished, and though born it is not born; for this reason, next the unsurpassed nature of *nirvāṇa* is explained.

Since that which has been taught is supreme, the benefits obtained are boundless; those who give rise to faith, make offerings, hear the Dharma, uphold it, and praise it, shall attain immeasurable merit. Manifesting supernatural powers, [the Buddha] cites the superior practices of others and human and dharmic phenomena as testimony. Furthermore, because of the power of long-practiced causes, they are able to transform others and receive [the teaching]; when the Noble One arrived from afar to inquire and hear the sutra, the Tathāgata rubbed the crown of his head and praised him earnestly three times. To clarify these excellent matters and cause them to flow forth universally, he next expounds the supreme and wondrous power. Thus, following the sequence of the flow, he next explains the unsurpassed supreme power.

The interpretations of various schools are infinite in their divergent views, and the emergence and disappearance of sūtras and śāstras occur through many gateways; the insights therein are immeasurable. Briefly following the sequence of my lectures, I have set forth a small portion of these matters. I do not wish to present the full extent of what I have heard, but have recorded only enough to meet the requirements of the occasion.
The End of the *Yijue* (Decisions on the Meaning) of the *Fahua Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
